We then set the 2030 revenue requirements by scaling up the 2019 component-level rates according to the growth shown in Figure 2, then multiplying the component-level rates by the total electricity demand in 2030 to get the 2030 revenue requirement in each cost category. The adjustment continues until the total revenue generated by applying the dynamic tariff aligns with the target revenue, based on the 2030 total utility load shape. One crucial factor in calculating tariffs is the hourly day-ahead wholesale price. The Avoided Cost Calculator (ACC) obtains these prices from Strategic Energy & Risk Valuation Model (SERVM), a simulation model representing an idealized view of the day-ahead market. However, these raw prices require adjustments to better reflect real-world conditions. SERVM offers a theoretical and optimized view of the day-ahead market. However, its cost estimates have been post-processed by E3 to reflect historical market behavior. This involves applying price caps and floors ($0/MWh to avoid curtailing renewables and $250/MWh for unprecedented high-price hours) and incorporating a scarcity scaling function that captures market non- idealities during peak hours. These adjustments are reported for NP-15 and SP-15 in 2030. These adjusted prices are reported for NP-15 and SP-15 zones in 2030. However, two issues prevent their direct use. First, SERVM's prices are based on its own modeled load and generation, which differ from our calculations using the LBNL DR-Path model. Second, SERVM's prices incorporate factors beyond net load, such as generator variable O&M costs, gas prices, carbon prices, and carbon intensity. These factors complicate the direct relationship between price and net load and fall outside our study's scope.
